parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at Fig. 6.1 with switch S at X. Which two capacitors share the same two junctions and so are in parallel with each other?
Hint 2: Once you have combined that parallel pair into a single value, that combination is in series with the remaining capacitor. Recall how to combine two capacitances in series.
parts.proper_answer: P and T in parallel give $2C$. In series with Q: $1/C_{total} = 1/C + 1/2C$, so $C_{total} = 2C/3$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Parallel Pair**
With S at X, the top wire from S joins the junction between P and Q to the top plate of T, and the bottom plates of P and T join at the battery negative. So P and T have the same p.d. across them. They are in parallel. For parallel, capacitances simply add: $$C_{P+T} = C + C = 2C$$

Step 2: **Add the Series Capacitor Q**
This $2C$ combination is in series with Q along the battery loop. For series, use reciprocals: $$\frac{1}{C_{total}} = \frac{1}{C_Q} + \frac{1}{C_{P+T}} = \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{2C} = \frac{3}{2C}$$ Invert to get: $$C_{total} = \frac{2C}{3}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: In a series path the charge stored on each series section must be the same. Think about finding the total charge supplied by the 9.0 V battery first.
Hint 2: That same total charge sits on capacitor Q alone. Use $Q = CV$ for Q to find its p.d., and remember larger capacitance means smaller p.d. for the same charge.
parts.proper_answer: Total charge $Q = C_{total}V = (2C/3) \times 9.0 = 6.0C$. This is the charge on Q, so $V_Q = Q/C = 6.0 \text{ V}$. The larger $2C$ parallel combination takes only $3.0 \text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Charge That Flows**
The battery sees the total capacitance $2C/3$ at $9.0 \text{ V}$. The charge delivered is: $$Q_{total} = C_{total}V = \left(\frac{2C}{3}\right) \times 9.0 = 6.0C$$ In series, charge is common. So capacitor Q carries this full charge $6.0C$, and the P+T parallel block as a whole also carries $6.0C$.

Step 2: **Convert Charge on Q to p.d.**
For Q alone, $Q = C V_Q$, so: $$V_Q = \frac{Q_{total}}{C} = \frac{6.0C}{C} = 6.0 \text{ V}$$ This makes sense: Q has the smaller capacitance ($C$ versus $2C$), so it takes the larger share of the $9.0 \text{ V}$. Check: $V_{P+T} = 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0 \text{ V}$.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: steady state blocking of d.c. by capacitor
hints: Hint 1: When S moves to Y, what is now connected directly across capacitor P? Think about a charged capacitor connected to a resistor with no battery in that local loop.
Hint 2: What happens to the charge and p.d. on a capacitor when it is left to discharge through a resistor for a long time?
Hint 3: After that discharge is complete, is there any continuous current in the main battery-Q-R loop? Remember a charged capacitor in series blocks steady d.c.
Hint 4: Apply Kirchhoff voltage law around the battery-Q-R loop with zero current and zero resistor drop to decide the final p.d. across Q.
parts.proper_answer: Capacitor P: p.d. falls to zero. P discharges through R. Capacitor Q: p.d. rises to $9.0 \text{ V}$. With no current in steady state there is no p.d. across R, so full e.m.f. appears across Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Capacitor P Discharges to Zero**
Moving S to Y puts resistor R directly in parallel with P. The $3.0 \text{ V}$ already on P drives a discharge current through R. Charge flows off the plates until P is fully discharged. So: $$V_P \to 0$$

Step 2: **No Steady Current Can Remain**
Capacitor Q is in series with the battery and R. Once transients die away, a capacitor blocks steady d.c., so the final current $I = 0$. That means there is no p.d. across the resistor: $$V_R = IR = 0$$

Step 3: **Capacitor Q Takes the Full e.m.f.**
Going round the loop, battery e.m.f. = $V_Q + V_R$. With $V_R = 0$ and $V_P = V_R = 0$ in parallel: $$V_Q = 9.0 \text{ V}$$ In words, Q charges up a little more from $6.0 \text{ V}$ to $9.0 \text{ V}$ while P empties from $3.0 \text{ V}$ to zero. Capacitor T is left isolated and keeps its charge.

Step 4: **Summary Picture**
Think of R as a leak for P but not a permanent drain on the battery. P: $3.0 \text{ V} \to 0$. Q: $6.0 \text{ V} \to 9.0 \text{ V}$.
